opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it helps to start with what a language model is actually doing. At every step it's choosing the next token from a vocabulary of maybe fifty or a hundred thousand options. That's a big number, but it's finite and discrete, and the output is essentially a one-dimensional sequence. One word after another.

Now think about a robot picking up a coffee mug. The robot has to produce a continuous trajectory for every joint, say seven joints on a typical arm plus the gripper, at hundreds of times per second. Each of those values is a real number, not a choice from a list. And that's just the robot's side. The world has its own state, much of which the robot can't see: where exactly the mug is, its mass distribution, how much liquid is inside and how it's sloshing, the friction coefficient of the ceramic, whether the handle is slightly chipped. Then contact happens, and contact is notoriously hard. Tiny differences in where fingertip meets surface lead to very different outcomes. The object might slide, rotate, or tip over. Small errors compound, and the physics is discontinuous in ways that are hard to model.

So you're going from a discrete, low-dimensional output space to a continuous, very high-dimensional space with uncertainty in perception, in control, and in the physics itself. That's a different kind of problem.

And dimensionality interacts with data. Roughly speaking, the amount of data you need grows dramatically with the number of dimensions you need to cover. Language models were trained on the internet. If you added up all the text they've seen, a human reading eight hours a day would need something like a hundred thousand years to get through it. For robot manipulation we have nothing remotely comparable. There's no internet of robot actions, no huge corpus of examples linking what a robot saw, what it did with its joints, and what happened. So the space we need to cover is far larger, and the data we have is far smaller. I call that the hundred-thousand-year data gap.

That's why I push back a bit when people say humanoid robots will be doing our laundry next year. Folding a shirt is a deformable object with effectively infinite degrees of freedom. A four-year-old can do it, but it's very hard for a robot. Moravec pointed this out decades ago: what's easy for us is hard for machines, and vice versa. Language turned out to be on the easier side of that divide, which surprised a lot of people. Manipulation is still on the hard side.

I'm optimistic we'll close the gap, through simulation, teleoperation, and good old-fashioned engineering combined with learning. But I think it'll take longer than the hype suggests, and dimensionality is a big part of why.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a robot’s joint values and the mug’s state, but never states that position and orientation in 3D require six degrees of freedom.

r002.rationale: It says the data needed grows dramatically with the number of dimensions, but does not state that possible robot configurations grow exponentially with degrees of freedom.

r003.rationale: It characterizes language output as a “one-dimensional sequence,” with “one word after another.”

r004.rationale: It contrasts continuous, high-dimensional robot output with discrete language output, but does not claim that physical-motion possibilities vastly exceed combinations of words into sentences.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me try to explain it this way. Think about what's happening with language. The input is text, a sequence of words, and the output is more text. Each word gets mapped into a very high dimensional vector space, that's all true, but the actual structure of the problem is quite compact. There's a finite vocabulary, there's a fixed grammar, and critically, there is this enormous reservoir of data, basically everything humans have ever written down, which lets you learn the statistics of that space extremely well. So language is high dimensional in one sense, but the data density is enormous, and that's what matters.

Now look at what a robot has to do when it picks something up. Just the simplest case, grasping an object on a table. Where's the gripper in space? That's six dimensions right there, three for position and three for orientation. Now what's the object? Its shape, its pose, its mass, how the mass is distributed, the friction between the fingers and the surface, and friction is notoriously hard to model. Is it rigid, is it deformable? Is there a second object next to it that will get knocked over? And then every one of those is uncertain. The robot's camera gives you a noisy, partial view. The motors have errors. So the state of the world lives in a very high dimensional continuous space, and the dimensionality of the control problem, the sequence of torques you have to send to the joints over time, that's another high dimensional continuous space on top of it.

And here's the key thing. We don't have the equivalent of the internet for that. Nobody has written down a trillion examples of how fingertips interact with a wine glass. The data you can collect comes from physical robots doing things, one trial at a time, in real time, and physics doesn't let you speed that up. So you have this combination of a space that's much bigger and far less structured, and a data set that's orders of magnitude smaller. That ratio is really what makes it hard.

This is essentially Moravec's paradox, which Hans Moravec pointed out back in the eighties. The things that seem hard for humans, like playing chess or writing an essay, turn out to be comparatively easy for computers, and the things a two year old does effortlessly, like picking up a spoon, turn out to be incredibly hard. And I think the dimensionality argument explains why. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years optimizing manipulation and perception. Language is maybe a hundred thousand years old. We're asking robots to catch up on the problem that took biology the longest to solve.

So when people see ChatGPT and ask, why don't we have robots that can fold laundry yet, that's the answer I give. It's not that we're not trying. It's that the problems are fundamentally different in their geometry.

r001.rationale: The response says a gripper’s position uses three dimensions and its orientation uses three more, totaling six.

r002.rationale: It describes the robot’s state and control spaces as high-dimensional, but does not say the number of possible configurations grows exponentially with degrees of freedom.

r003.rationale: It describes language input as text arranged as a sequence of words, conveying a linear sequence.

r004.rationale: It contrasts robotics’ larger, less structured space with language’s abundant data, but does not claim physical motion possibilities vastly outnumber possible word combinations into sentences.

astra-6.text:
Well, one way to think about it is to consider the space of possible actions. In language, you’re choosing from a finite vocabulary. There are many possible sequences, of course, but each next token is a discrete choice.

With a robot, even specifying the position and orientation of its hand takes six dimensions: three for position and three for orientation. Then you have the joints of the fingers, the forces you’re applying, and how all of those change over time. Those variables are continuous, and they interact. When you touch an object, a small change in where you make contact can make a big difference to what happens.

And if the object is deformable—say, a shirt—you can’t describe it with just a position and an orientation. You have to represent its shape, all those folds, and how they’ll change when you pull on one corner. The dimensionality grows enormously.

That doesn’t mean language is easy. But physical manipulation involves searching through this very high-dimensional space while working with incomplete observations. You can’t see every contact, you don’t know the friction exactly, and you still have to choose an action that works in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response assigns six dimensions to the robot hand’s position and orientation, not an object’s.

r002.rationale: It describes a high-dimensional space but does not say the number of robot configurations grows exponentially with degrees of freedom.

r003.rationale: It mentions token sequences and next-token choices, but does not characterize word arrangement as one-dimensional or linear.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the number of physical motion possibilities with the possible word combinations into sentences.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about it is to look at the space of possible actions. With language, you have a finite vocabulary, and you’re producing a sequence of discrete tokens. That can express extraordinarily complex ideas, but the interface is relatively constrained.

For a robot, even positioning a rigid object involves six dimensions: three for position and three for orientation. Then you have the joints of the robot, the configuration of its fingers, and all the different ways it might make contact with the object. If the object is something deformable, like a shirt or a cable, the number of dimensions grows enormously.

And you don’t get to observe all of those dimensions directly. You have images, you have noisy measurements, and you have to infer what’s happening. When you touch something, it moves, so your action changes the situation you’re trying to understand.

That’s not a proof that manipulation is harder than language in every sense. But it helps explain why generating a plausible description of how to fold a shirt is very different from actually folding one. The robot has to make the geometry, the contact, and the physics all work together.

r001.rationale: It says positioning a rigid object involves six dimensions: three for position and three for orientation.

r002.rationale: It says the number of dimensions grows enormously for deformable objects, but does not state that possible robot configurations grow exponentially with degrees of freedom.

r003.rationale: It describes language as a sequence of discrete tokens, but does not characterize the arrangement as one-dimensional or linear.

r004.rationale: It contrasts constrained language output with the complexity of physical manipulation, but does not claim that motion possibilities vastly exceed sentence combinations.
